title: Essays vs reports
examples: When should I use a report instead of an essay?
What is the difference in tone between the two?
Can I mix the structure of both in one paper?

explain.say: Today we look at essays and reports. Both are common academic writing formats. Knowing when to use which is important.

draw.text: Essay vs Report: Structure, Purpose, Tone

explain.say: The structure guides how you organize your ideas. Essays usually have an introduction, body, and conclusion. Reports often include sections like an executive summary and methodology.

draw.text: Structure: Intro, Body, Conclusion vs Sections

explain.say: The purpose defines what you want to achieve with your writing. An essay aims to persuade the reader of your specific argument. A report aims to present impartial findings about a situation.
Tone refers to the writer's attitude toward the subject. Essays can allow for a more interpretive or critical tone. Reports must maintain a formal and neutral tone always.
In real life, imagine you are advising a company. If you need to convince the board to adopt a new policy, write an essay. If you are simply presenting the results of a market survey, write a report.

items: Convince board of new policy: Essay

explain.say: A common mistake is using emotional language in a report. Remember reports require you to stick strictly to the evidence you have found. Always keep your personal feelings out of the findings.

faq.q: Do I need a bibliography for both essays and reports?
faq.a: Yes, you need a bibliography for both formats. You must always credit your sources properly to avoid plagiarism.

faq.q: If my essay is about research, should I write it like a report?
faq.a: It depends on the prompt. If the task is 'Analyze the findings...', use an essay. If it is 'Investigate and report on...', use a report.
asks: Which format is better for research?
Does the topic determine the format?

faq.q: Can I use informal language in my academic writing?
faq.a: No, academic writing requires a formal tone. Avoid slang, contractions, and overly casual phrasing in both essays and reports.
asks: Is it okay to sound like myself?
What is the right tone for university?

faq.q: Is the structure the most important thing to remember?
faq.a: No, the purpose is the most important guide. Understanding why you are writing dictates whether you need to persuade or just inform.
asks: What should I focus on first?

faq.q: What is the main difference in the conclusion?
faq.a: In an essay, the conclusion summarizes arguments and restates the thesis. In a report, it summarizes findings and offers clear recommendations.
asks: How do I end a report?
What is the final step for each?

facts: Essays are primarily designed to explore and argue a viewpoint.
Reports are designed to present factual findings based on investigation.
A formal tone is required for both academic essays and reports.
Reports often include a section detailing the research methodology used.

quiz.say: You are writing a paper to convince your professor that a certain historical event was misunderstood. Which format is best?
quiz.why: An essay is designed to build and argue a specific viewpoint or thesis.

wrong.0: Both formats are appropriate if the goal is persuasion.
wrong.2: Reports are for presenting objective findings, not personal arguments.
wrong.3: The format must match the primary goal of the writing task.

quiz.say: Your task is to present the raw data collected from a recent environmental impact survey. What should your writing focus on?
quiz.why: A report's purpose is to objectively present the findings gathered from data collection.

wrong.0: An essay would try to argue the meaning of the data, not just present it.
wrong.1: A memo is usually for internal communication, not formal academic submission.
wrong.2: A letter is too personal for presenting broad survey results.

quiz.say: If you write, 'It is clear that the results show...', which tone are you using?
quiz.why: Using phrases like 'the data suggests' maintains a formal and objective tone.

wrong.1: Interpretive tone suggests your personal reading of the evidence.
wrong.2: Persuasive tone tries to make the reader agree with you immediately.
wrong.3: Informal tone uses casual language unsuitable for university work.
